[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 06 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is our graduate teaching assistant, Sora. Hello everyone! Today, we complete Section 1.2 on workbook pages 10 and 11: Negative Exponents, Power Rules, and Master Simplifications.

[TA Sora] Today is where all our exponent knowledge comes together into an unstoppable algebraic toolkit. Students are often frightened when they first see negative exponentsâthey mistakenly assume that a negative exponent turns the entire number negative. That is completely untrue!

[Prof. Park] A negative exponent has nothing to do with whether a number is positive or negative. A negative exponent is simply an elevator pass: it tells a factor to take the elevator across the fraction bar to the opposite floor! That is such an intuitive analogy, Sora!

[TA Sora] Right here in Bozeman, our local optics and photonics industryâoften called 'Photonics Valley'âdevelops ultra-precise lasers for scientific research, atmospheric monitoring, and aerospace sensors.

[Prof. Park] Engineers measuring laser wavelengths routinely work with numbers like 5 times 10 to the negative 7 meters, and semiconductor physicists measure electron mass at 9.1 times 10 to the negative 31 kilograms. Negative exponents represent small, precision scales, not negative debt.

[TA Sora] Today, we will master the elevator rule, the power of a power rule, and tackle the grand master multi-variable simplifications on workbook page 11. Let's begin on slide 2!

title: The Negative Exponent Rule ($a^{-m} = \frac{1}{a^m}$): The Elevator Metaphor
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Rule Reference (Workbook p. 8 & 10)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
$$\text{Negative Exponent Definition: } \quad a^{-m} = \dfrac{1}{a^m} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \dfrac{1}{a^{-m}} = a^m$$

$$\text{Fraction Reciprocal Property: } \quad \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{-m} = \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^m$$
solution: $$\mathbf{\text{A negative exponent does NOT make a number negative—it triggers a reciprocal!}}$$
pitfall:
**SORA'S ELEVATOR METAPHOR:**
- Think of the fraction bar as an elevator floor!
- A term with a negative exponent is unhappy on its current floor.
- Move it across the fraction bar (up or down), and its exponent turns **POSITIVE**!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 2, we introduce the Negative Exponent Property: a^(-n) = 1 / (a^n), and conversely 1 / (a^(-n)) = a^n, where the base a is non-zero. Sora, explain the elevator ticket rule in detail for our students.

[TA Sora] Think of a fraction as a two-story building: the penthouse upstairs is the numerator, and the ground floor downstairs is the denominator. Whenever a factor has a negative exponent, it is unhappy with its current floor!

[Prof. Park] Its negative sign is literally a ticket that says: 'Move me to the other floor!' If an expression like x^(-3) is upstairs in the numerator, you move it downstairs to the denominator, and upon arrival, the ticket is punchedâthe negative exponent turns into a positive 3: 1 / (x^3).

[TA Sora] And what happens if the negative exponent is already downstairs in the denominator, like 1 / (y^(-4))? Then it takes the elevator upstairs to the numerator! It becomes y^(+4) in the penthouse, and its denominator becomes 1.

[Prof. Park] Notice two crucial golden rules: First, moving a factor across the fraction bar changes ONLY the sign of the exponent, NEVER the sign of the base! If you have (-5)^(-3), the negative 5 stays negative 5âit simply moves downstairs as 1 / [ (-5)^3 ].

[TA Sora] Second, only factors with negative exponents move. Factors with positive exponents stay right where they are. Let's practice with Example 4 on slide 3!

title: Section 1.2 Example 4 (Parts A & B): Basic Negative Powers
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 4 A & B (Workbook p. 10)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Example 4: Simplify using only positive integer exponents (Workbook p. 10):**

$$\text{A. } 12x^{-4} \qquad \text{B. } 3a^{-2} b^9$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Part A: } & 12x^{-4} \\
& \text{Notice: The exponent } -4 \text{ applies ONLY to } x, \text{ NOT the 12!} \\
& 12 \text{ stays in numerator: } 12 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^4} = \mathbf{\dfrac{12}{x^4}} \\[1em]
\text{Part B: } & 3a^{-2} b^9 \\
& 3 \text{ and } b^9 \text{ have positive exponents (stay on top).} \\
& a^{-2} \text{ travels down to denominator: } \mathbf{\dfrac{3b^9}{a^2}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**THE COEFFICIENT TRAP IN PART A:**
- Do NOT move 12 to the bottom! 12 has an exponent of $+1$ ($12^1$).
- Only the variable with the negative exponent moves: $\mathbf{\frac{12}{x^4}}$, NOT $\frac{1}{12x^4}$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Let's examine Section 1.2 Example 4 Parts A, B, and C on workbook page 10: Part A: x^(-4). Part B: 3^(-2). Part C: (-5)^(-2). In Part A, x^(-4) is in the numerator. We send x downstairs to the denominator, and the exponent becomes positive 4: 1 / (x^4).

[TA Sora] Simple, clean, and done! Now look at Part B: 3^(-2). A common student mistake is to multiply 3 by -2 and write -6. That is completely wrong! The negative sign belongs to the exponent, so it sends the base 3 downstairs: 1 / (3^2).

[Prof. Park] Now 3 squared is 9, so our answer is 1/9! Notice that 1/9 is a positive fractionâthe negative exponent never made the number negative. Now compare Part B with Part C: (-5)^(-2). Here, the base is -5 inside parentheses.

[TA Sora] The negative exponent -2 sends the entire base (-5) downstairs: 1 / [ (-5)^2 ]. Downstairs, (-5)^2 is (-5)(-5) = +25! So our final answer is 1/25. Sora, what happens if someone asks about 0^(-2)? Can zero have a negative exponent? That is a brilliant question!

[Prof. Park] If you try 0^(-2), the elevator rule sends zero downstairs: 1 / (0^2) = 1/0! And from Lecture 02, we know dividing by zero is strictly UNDEFINED! That is why our exponent property explicitly specifies that the base a can NEVER be zero.

[TA Sora] For all non-zero bases, the elevator rule works flawlessly and predictably every single time.

title: Section 1.2 Example 4 (Parts C & D): Fractions & Grouped Powers
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 4 C & D (Workbook p. 10)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Example 4: Simplify using only positive integer exponents (Workbook p. 10):**

$$\text{C. } \left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right)^{-2} \qquad \text{D. } (4y)^{-3}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Part C: } & \left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right)^{-2} \\
& \text{Apply fraction reciprocal rule (flip inside, make exponent positive):} \\
& \left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right)^{-2} = \left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{8^2}{5^2} = \mathbf{\dfrac{64}{25}} \\[1em]
\text{Part D: } & (4y)^{-3} \\
& \text{The entire group } (4y) \text{ is in parentheses: move the whole group down:} \\
& \dfrac{1}{(4y)^3} = \dfrac{1}{4^3 \cdot y^3} = \mathbf{\dfrac{1}{64y^3}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**CONTRAST $(4y)^{-3}$ vs. $4y^{-3}$:**
- In $(4y)^{-3}$, the 4 is inside parentheses, so $4^3 = 64$ is on the bottom: $\mathbf{\frac{1}{64y^3}}$.
- Without parentheses ($4y^{-3}$), 4 would stay on top: $\frac{4}{y^3}$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Now let's examine Example 4 Parts D, E, and F on slide 4: Part D: -5^(-2). Part E: 1 / (x^(-6)). Part F: (2/3)^(-3). Look at Part D: -5^(-2) without parentheses!

[TA Sora] Remember our base identification rule from Lecture 02: the exponent -2 applies ONLY to the number 5, NOT the negative sign out front! So the negative sign stays out front as -1. The 5 moves downstairs: - [ 1 / (5^2) ] = -1/25.

[Prof. Park] Compare Part C: (-5)^(-2) = +1/25, whereas Part D: -5^(-2) = -1/25. That distinction is guaranteed to appear on your exam! Now look at Part E: 1 / (x^(-6)). Here, x^(-6) is downstairs in the denominator.

[TA Sora] It takes the elevator upstairs to the numerator, and the exponent becomes positive 6: x^6 / 1 = x^6! And look at Part F: (2/3)^(-3). A fraction raised to a negative power!

[Prof. Park] When an entire fraction is raised to a negative exponent, the negative power flips the entire fraction to its reciprocal! (2/3)^(-3) becomes (3/2)^(+3). Now cube both top and bottom: 3^3 / 2^3 = 27/8! Flipping the fraction uses up the negative sign instantly. What a brilliant shortcut!

[TA Sora] Think of it as turning an hourglass upside down: the sand that was on top is now on the bottom, and the timer starts fresh. Whenever an entire rational fraction is wrapped in parentheses with a negative power, flip first, then distribute.

title: Section 1.2 Example 4 (Parts E & F): Denominator Negatives & Multi-Variables
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 4 E & F (Workbook p. 10)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Example 4: Simplify using only positive integer exponents (Workbook p. 10):**

$$\text{E. } \dfrac{n^{10}}{p^{-10}} \qquad \text{F. } \dfrac{15r^{-4}s^8}{3s r^3}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Part E: } & \dfrac{n^{10}}{p^{-10}} \\
& p^{-10} \text{ is in the denominator with a negative power: ride elevator UP!} \\
& \mathbf{n^{10} p^{10}} \\[1em]
\text{Part F: } & \dfrac{15r^{-4}s^8}{3s r^3} \\
& \text{Step 1: Reduce coefficients: } \dfrac{15}{3} = \mathbf{5} \\
& \text{Step 2: Move } r^{-4} \text{ to denominator: } r^3 \cdot r^4 = r^{3+4} = \mathbf{r^7} \quad (\text{in denominator}) \\
& \text{Step 3: Simplify } s \ (s = s^1): \dfrac{s^8}{s^1} = s^{8-1} = \mathbf{s^7} \quad (\text{in numerator}) \\[0.5em]
& \text{Final Result: } \mathbf{\dfrac{5s^7}{r^7}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Pro-Tip for Part F:** Moving $r^{-4}$ to the bottom immediately turns it into $r^4$, which joins $r^3$ to give $r^7$ without confusing negative subtraction!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 introduces the Power Rules: 1. Power of a Power: (a^m)^n = a^(m Â· n). 2. Power of a Product: (ab)^n = a^n Â· b^n. 3. Power of a Quotient: (a/b)^n = a^n / b^n. Let's explain why (a^m)^n means multiplying exponents! Take (a^2)^3. What does that mean?

[TA Sora] It means taking three copies of a^2: (a^2) Â· (a^2) Â· (a^2). By the product rule from Lecture 05, we add: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, which is 2 times 3!

[Prof. Park] So when a power is raised to another power, you MULTIPLY the exponents: a^(2 Â· 3) = a^6. And when you have multiple factors inside parentheses raised to an outside power, like (2x^3)^4, the outside exponent distributes to EVERY single factor insideâincluding the numerical coefficient!

[TA Sora] So (2x^3)^4 = 2^4 Â· (x^3)^4 = 16 x^(3 Â· 4) = 16x^12. Never forget the coefficient! Students often write 2x^12, forgetting to raise 2 to the 4th power. Every citizen inside the parentheses gets hit by the outside exponent.

[Prof. Park] Think of the outside exponent as rain falling on an open picnic tableâeverything on the table gets wet! Even in scientific notation, when you square (3 Â· 10^4)^2, you square 3 to get 9, and multiply exponents 4 Â· 2 = 8, giving 9 Â· 10^8.

[TA Sora] Treating every factor inside with equal respect guarantees no term is left unscaled.

title: Section 1.2 Example 5 (Parts A & B): Power to a Power Rule
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 5 A & B (Workbook p. 11)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Part A: } & (5x^4)^2 \\
& \text{Apply outer exponent 2 to coefficient and variable:} \\
& 5^2 \cdot (x^4)^2 = 25 \cdot x^{4 \cdot 2} = \mathbf{25x^8} \\[1em]
\text{Part B: } & (-2x^3 y^7)^3 \\
& \text{Apply outer exponent 3 to all three factors:} \\
& (-2)^3 \cdot (x^3)^3 \cdot (y^7)^3 = (-8) \cdot x^{3 \cdot 3} \cdot y^{7 \cdot 3} = \mathbf{-8x^9 y^{21}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**THE COEFFICIENT POWER TRAP:**
- In Part A: $5^2 = 25$, NEVER $5 \times 2 = 10$!
- In Part B: $(-2)^3 = (-2)(-2)(-2) = -8$, NEVER $-6$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Let's look at Example 5 Parts A and B on slide 6: Part A: (y^4)^5. Part B: (-2a^3)^4. In Part A, (y^4)^5 is a textbook power of a power. We multiply the inside exponent by the outside exponent: 4 Â· 5 = 20. So our result is y^20.

[TA Sora] Done in one clean step! Now look at Part B: (-2a^3)^4. Here, the negative 2 is inside the parentheses, and the outside exponent is 4. We distribute the exponent 4 to both parts: First, (-2)^4. Since the exponent 4 is even, (-2)(-2)(-2)(-2) = +16.

[Prof. Park] Second, (a^3)^4 = a^(3 Â· 4) = a^12. Combine them: +16a^12. Notice that an even power turns a negative coefficient positive: (-2)^4 = +16. If the outside power had been 3 (an odd power), (-2)^3 would have remained negative 8: -8a^9. And what if there were no parentheses: -2(a^3)^4?

[TA Sora] Then the 4 would only apply to a^3, giving -2a^12! Even powers absorb negatives inside parentheses; odd powers preserve them. Keep that rule in mind for rapid mental checking!

[Prof. Park] In Bozeman's precision photonics sector, optical engineers calculate laser pulse frequencies where wavelengths scale as powers of 10 to the negative 6 meters. If an engineer forgets to distribute an outer negative power across numerical coefficients or drops an elevator sign, an entire optical sensor calibration is ruined! Exactly, Professor!

[TA Sora] That is why I always tell students: treat exponents like bank transaction entries. Every negative exponent is a pending wire transfer across the fraction bar line. Once it crosses over, the fee is paid and the sign becomes positive!

title: Section 1.2 Example 5 (Parts C & D): Nested Powers & Monomial Fractions
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 5 C & D (Workbook p. 11)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Part C: } & (a^9 b^6)^5 = a^{9 \cdot 5} \cdot b^{6 \cdot 5} = \mathbf{a^{45} b^{30}} \\[1em]
\text{Part D: } & \dfrac{w^3 \cdot w^9}{(w^5)^4} \\
& \text{Numerator (Product Rule: ADD): } w^3 \cdot w^9 = w^{3+9} = w^{12} \\
& \text{Denominator (Power Rule: MULTIPLY): } (w^5)^4 = w^{5 \cdot 4} = w^{20} \\[0.5em]
& \text{Apply Quotient Rule: } \dfrac{w^{12}}{w^{20}} = \dfrac{1}{w^{20-12}} = \mathbf{\dfrac{1}{w^8}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**ADD vs. MULTIPLY IN PART D:**
- On top: $w^3 \cdot w^9 \implies$ multiplying bases means **ADD** exponents ($3+9=12$).
- On bottom: $(w^5)^4 \implies$ power to power means **MULTIPLY** exponents ($5 \times 4 = 20$)!
script:
[Prof. Park] Moving to slide 7 with Example 5 Parts C and D: Part C: (a^9 b^6)^5. Part D: (w^3 Â· w^8) / (w^5)^2. In Part C, (a^9 b^6)^5 has two variable factors inside. Distribute the outside exponent 5 to both: For a: (a^9)^5 = a^(9 Â· 5) = a^45.

[TA Sora] For b: (b^6)^5 = b^(6 Â· 5) = b^30. So our simplified term is a^45 b^30! Now look at Part D: (w^3 Â· w^8) / (w^5)^2. Here we combine the product rule, the power of a power rule, and the quotient rule!

[Prof. Park] Let's simplify top and bottom separately: In the numerator: w^3 Â· w^8 = w^(3 + 8) = w^11. In the denominator: (w^5)^2 = w^(5 Â· 2) = w^10. Now we have w^11 / w^10. Apply the quotient rule: 11 - 10 = 1.

[TA Sora] So w^11 / w^10 = w^1 = w! Look how an expression with four exponents collapsed down to a single letter w. That is mathematical elegance in action. If someone tested this with w = 2: numerator would be 2^3 Â· 2^8 = 8 Â· 256 = 2048.

[Prof. Park] Denominator: (2^5)^2 = 32^2 = 1024. 2048 divided by 1024 is exactly 2! The algebra works flawlessly with actual numbers.

[TA Sora] Here is an extra pro-tip for slide 7: whenever you have a fraction with multiple variables and coefficients raised to a negative power outside, you can also flip the ENTIRE fraction upside down right at the start to turn the outer exponent positive!

[Prof. Park] That is the Fraction Inversion Property: (A/B)^(-n) = (B/A)^n! In our problem, flipping the fraction first gives [ z^(-4) / (3 x^(-2) y) ]^3, which leads to the exact same final answer: x^6 / (27 y^3 z^12).

[TA Sora] Having two independent ways to solve a problem is the greatest confidence builder in algebra!

title: Section 1.2 Example 5 (Part E): Product of Monomial Quotients
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 5 E (Workbook p. 11)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Example 5 Part E (Workbook p. 11):** Simplify fully:

$\mathbf{\left(\dfrac{2x^6 w^5}{3x w^5}\right)\left(\dfrac{7x^5 w^2}{9x^2}\right)}$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Simplify the first parenthetical fraction:} \\
& w^5 \text{ cancels completely } \left(\dfrac{w^5}{w^5} = 1\right), \quad \dfrac{x^6}{x^1} = x^5 \implies \mathbf{\dfrac{2x^5}{3}} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Simplify the second parenthetical fraction:} \\
& \dfrac{x^5}{x^2} = x^3 \implies \mathbf{\dfrac{7x^3 w^2}{9}} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Multiply the simplified fractions straight across:} \\
& \left(\dfrac{2x^5}{3}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{7x^3 w^2}{9}\right) = \dfrac{(2 \cdot 7) \cdot (x^{5+3}) \cdot w^2}{3 \cdot 9} = \mathbf{\dfrac{14x^8 w^2}{27}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**SIMPLIFY INSIDE FIRST:**
- Always cancel common factors inside each group first before multiplying across! Look how $w^5$ vanished immediately!
script:
[Prof. Park] Now let's tackle Example 5 Part E on slide 8: Simplify fully: [ (2 x^6 w^5) / (3 x w^5) ]^3.

[TA Sora] When you have a fraction inside parentheses raised to an outside power, you have two choices: Choice 1: Distribute the power 3 to every single factor on top and bottom first. Choice 2: SIMPLIFY INSIDE FIRST, then raise to the power 3!

[Prof. Park] Sora's Golden Rule: ALWAYS simplify inside the parentheses first! It shrinks your numbers before you raise them to powers. Let's follow Sora's advice and simplify inside first: Look at the w terms: w^5 on top and w^5 on the bottom. w^5 / w^5 = 1! They cancel out completely!

[TA Sora] Look at the x terms: x^6 on top and x^1 on the bottom. By the quotient rule: 6 - 1 = 5, so x^5 remains on top. The coefficients 2 and 3 cannot be reduced. So inside the parentheses, we are left with: (2x^5 / 3)!

[Prof. Park] Look how much smaller that is! Now apply the outside cube 3 to everything: Numerator: 2^3 Â· (x^5)^3 = 8 x^(5 Â· 3) = 8x^15. Denominator: 3^3 = 27. Our final answer is: (8x^15) / 27.

[TA Sora] If we had distributed the cube first, we would have had 2^3 = 8, x^18, w^15 over 27 x^3 w^15, and then canceled. Simplifying inside first was much cleaner and saved us two full steps!

title: Section 1.2 Example 5 (Part F): Grand Master Exponent Simplification
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 06 • Section 1.2 Example 5 F (Workbook p. 11)
detail: Lecture 06: Zero & Negative Exponents: Simplifying Monomials
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Example 5 Part F (Workbook p. 11):** Simplify fully:

$\mathbf{\left(\dfrac{3x^{11}y^5}{2x^{-1}y^8}\right)\left(\dfrac{2x^5 y^{12}}{5x}\right)}$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Pre-cancel common numerical factor of 2 between numerator and denominator:} \\
& \text{The 2 in the first denominator and the 2 in the second numerator cancel!} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Move } x^{-1} \text{ up to numerator: } x^{11} \cdot x^1 = x^{12} \\
& \text{Multiply across numerators: } 3 \cdot x^{12} \cdot x^5 \cdot y^5 \cdot y^{12} = 3 x^{17} y^{17} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Multiply denominators: } 1 \cdot y^8 \cdot 5x = 5x y^8 \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 4: } & \text{Simplify the combined quotient:} \\
& \text{Coefficients: } \dfrac{3}{5} \\
& \text{Base } x: \dfrac{x^{17}}{x^1} = x^{17-1} = \mathbf{x^{16}} \\
& \text{Base } y: \dfrac{y^{17}}{y^8} = y^{17-8} = \mathbf{y^9} \\[0.8em]
\text{Final Result: } & \mathbf{\dfrac{3x^{16} y^9}{5}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**THE ULTIMATE EXAM PROBLEM:**
- This problem synthesizes negative exponents, product rule, quotient rule, and cross-canceling all at once.
- Follow the step-by-step pipeline: cancel numbers, move negatives, combine tops/bottoms, and simplify!
script:
[Prof. Park] Now we arrive at the ultimate master problem on slide 9: Example 5 Part F on workbook page 11: Simplify fully: [ (3 x^11 y^5) / (2 x^(-1) y^8) ]^(-2). This is the grand championship problem of Section 1.2!

[TA Sora] It has coefficients, positive exponents, negative exponents inside, and an outside negative exponent. Let's attack it methodically using our three-step protocol: Step 1: Simplify inside the parentheses first! Let's do that! Look at x: we have x^11 on top and x^(-1) on the bottom.

[Prof. Park] The x^(-1) on the bottom takes the elevator upstairs to the numerator and becomes x^(+1)! Upstairs, we already have x^11, so x^11 Â· x^1 = x^(11 + 1) = x^12. Now look at y: y^5 on top and y^8 on the bottom.

[TA Sora] 8 - 5 = 3, so y^3 stays on the bottom. So inside our parentheses, we now have: (3 x^12) / (2 y^3). Step 2: Look at the outside exponent: it is -2!

[Prof. Park] The negative sign on the outside exponent flips the entire inside fraction to its reciprocal: [ (2 y^3) / (3 x^12) ]^(+2)! Step 3: Now square every factor inside: Numerator: 2^2 Â· (y^3)^2 = 4 y^(3 Â· 2) = 4 y^6.

[TA Sora] Denominator: 3^2 Â· (x^12)^2 = 9 x^(12 Â· 2) = 9 x^24. Assemble the final fraction: (4 y^6) / (9 x^24)! Every exponent is positive, coefficients 4 and 9 share no common factors, and each variable appears once. Perfection!

script:
[Prof. Park] What a triumph! On slide 10, we synthesize all 5 examples from Section 1.2 into our Master Summary Table. Sora, let's review the final golden rules. 1. Zero Exponent: a^0 = 1 (for non-zero base). 2. Product Rule: multiplying identical bases -> ADD exponents. 3.

[TA Sora] Quotient Rule: dividing identical bases -> SUBTRACT exponents. 4. Negative Exponents: the elevator ruleâmove across the fraction bar to turn positive. 5. Power of a Power: multiply exponents. 6. Power of a Fraction: simplify inside first, flip if the outside power is negative, then distribute to every factor.
